questions.q: What naming pattern does every PowerShell cmdlet follow, and why does it matter?
options: Verb-Noun — a deliberate design choice that makes cmdlets guessable by pattern instead of requiring memorization
Noun-Verb, purely as a stylistic convention with no practical benefit
Cmdlets have no consistent naming pattern at all
Every cmdlet is named after the person who wrote it
questions.explain: PowerShell maintains an approved list of verbs, so once you know a handful you can often guess the cmdlet you need.

questions.q: What does a parameter like -Path do in a cmdlet call?
options: Tells the cmdlet what to act on, such as which folder to look in
Changes the cmdlet's verb to a different one
Has no effect on how the cmdlet runs
Is only valid inside the PowerShell ISE
questions.explain: Parameters start with a dash and specify what the cmdlet should act on, like Get-ChildItem -Path "C:\Logs".

questions.q: What is a switch parameter, such as -Recurse or -Force?
options: A parameter that takes no value — its presence alone turns on a behavior
A parameter that always requires a numeric value
A parameter that can only be used with Get- cmdlets
A deprecated feature no longer supported in PowerShell
questions.explain: Switch parameters like -Recurse or -Force are on/off — just including them changes the cmdlet's behavior.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why are named parameters the safer choice for a saved script compared to positional parameters?
options: They're self-documenting and don't silently break if parameters are reordered or new ones are added
Positional parameters are always faster to execute
Named parameters are required by PowerShell and positional ones don't actually work
There is no real difference between the two approaches
questions.explain: Named parameters make a script's intent explicit and resilient to reordering, which matters once a script gets saved and reused.

options: A switch parameter that skips the confirmation prompt
The name of the service being restarted
That the command will only run in the ISE
A required positional parameter
questions.explain: -Force is a switch — its presence alone tells the cmdlet to proceed without asking for confirmation.
